risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_marshall_2011 (ROBINS-I, first pass): serious, from confounding. An unadjusted comparison of two periods with no earlier trend, in an area chosen for its high overdose mortality; changes in the same area over the same years (more supportive housing and a 14% rise in population, police referral of people injecting in public to the site) are bundled with the opening, and others (supply, treatment, migration) are argued from other studies or measured only among the site's clients; deaths are placed by where they happened, not by who used the site. The outcome data are strong (all coroner-ruled deaths, unchanged criteria) and the 500 m radius was fixed in advance. A published letter adds a police operation around the site in 2003 and a fall in heroin supply around 2001 as changes at the same time, the first resting on an unnamed personal communication and the second on a cohort's self-reported overdoses and on markers in a 2006 paper (deaths across the province, naloxone use, seizures, self-reported daily heroin injection) that measured no heroin purity or price; the authors' reply cites a police evaluation for the operation having ended within weeks and its own reports of stable daily heroin use (Christian et al., 2012; Marshall et al., 2012). The two cited papers on file measured neither heroin availability or purity nor overdose deaths: they show a fall in self-reported non-fatal overdoses in a Vancouver cohort, largest between 2001 and 2002, inside the before period (Kerr et al., 2007), and a police crackdown in the Downtown Eastside from April 2003, also inside the before period, after which more people living there reported changing where they used drugs and discarded syringes shifted within the neighbourhood (Wood et al., 2004). The third, now read (Wood et al., 2006), measured neither heroin purity nor price: across British Columbia, overdose deaths fell mostly from 1998 to 2000, were about level in 2001 and lower in 2002 and 2003; ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside fell in every fiscal year to 2002–03, a fall under way in the site's neighbourhood during the before period that an unadjusted two-period comparison cannot separate from the opening (whether the rest of the city fell alike is not shown); and it does not contain the figures the study cites it for on stable drug use and methadone treatment from 2001 to 2005. None of this changes the judgment, which already rests on unmeasured changes at the same time.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for one site, its 500 m area and 2001–2005, with the drugs named as the coroners recorded them; it does not say how sites elsewhere, or a drug supply with fentanyl, would compare, which the paper does not address.

imprecision.note: 56 and 33 deaths near the site; the interval for the 35% fall reaches 0.0%, the test of the difference between the two areas' absolute falls gives p=0.049 (their relative falls do not differ significantly, p about 0.20, editors' calculation), and with the population held at its 2001 level the fall (30%) is not statistically significant.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; the authors' search found no other peer-reviewed study of a site's effect on overdose deaths up to December 2009.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the rate ratio near the site (0.65, editors' calculation) is not below 0.5, and the comparison is unadjusted.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the larger falls in census tracts nearer the site come from an exploratory fit, and the evidence is already rated down for risk of bias.

rate.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an unadjusted before-and-after comparison with changes at the same time) and one for imprecision (few deaths, an interval reaching no fall, a borderline difference between the areas in absolute falls only, and a fall near the site that loses significance when the population is held constant): very low. Rated as worded: an association between the opening of one site and a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 m than elsewhere in Vancouver in 2001–2005; not that supervised injection sites reduce deaths, nor that people who used the site were less likely to die, which the study did not measure. The authors' discussion calls such facilities safe and effective; 'safe' rests on other studies they cite, not on these data, and their conclusion asks that sites be considered for assessment. The drugs: opioids contributed to about half of the deaths and cocaine to about 6 in 10 (editors' sums; a death can involve both), and people at the site injected mostly heroin and powder cocaine; the paper does not mention fentanyl, so it says nothing about a supply in which fentanyl is common. Status single study. Now read against the published letter (Christian et al., 2012) and the authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012), from their PDFs (METHODS §2.3): rating and status unchanged. The letter disputes the cause of the fall, which the claim does not assert, and names two further changes at the same time (a police operation around the site in 2003 and a fall in heroin supply around 2001), now in the statement; it is entered as argument, attributed, since its own data are counts for areas larger than the study's, its police figures rest on an unnamed personal communication and its other figures are second-hand. The study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the 2001 start, and in the letter's own figure the drop from 2001 to 2002 is large in the Vancouver series (about 89 to 49 deaths) and small in the Downtown Eastside series (about 31 to 27; editors' reading). The reply answers the points on area, kinds of death and rates, and adds one restricted reanalysis of the same records (36%, no interval or comparison area), which is not independent replication; its answers on heroin and policing rest on its authors' own reports and a police evaluation, not read here; it leaves the 2001 start, the non-fatal overdose trend and the share of deaths without signs of injection elsewhere unanswered; and its call for such facilities to be central to responses goes beyond the paper's own call for assessment. Which deaths the letter's Downtown Eastside series counts cannot be settled from the two letters (a coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths, by the letter; vital statistics including suicides, by the reply). Also read against the two papers the letter cites that are on file (Kerr et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2004), from their PDFs: rating and status unchanged. Neither measured heroin availability or purity or overdose deaths, and neither reports figures for the study's two areas (within 500 m of the site and the rest of the city), so neither tests the letter's explanations or the study's association. The cohort's fall in self-reported non-fatal overdoses, largest between 2001 and 2002, is a fact about the background in the study's before period, which began in 2001: it fits the letter's point that 2001 was a high year in that cohort, but the study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the same start, the cohort is not split by area, and its authors' reasons (heroin supply, methadone) are suggestions without data on supply. The crackdown began inside the before period, and in its first three months more people living in the Downtown Eastside reported changing where they used drugs and discarded syringes shifted from its core to the rest of the neighbourhood; whether added police stayed after the opening (the letter) or left within weeks of it (the reply), neither paper shows. The letter departs from both papers in places: the cohort's question covered 6 months, not 12; its authors offer reduced supply only as a possible reason, alongside methadone; and the syringe counts that rose were in the rest of the Downtown Eastside, the only area counted, not in other areas of Vancouver (the paper's own abstract speaks of displacement into adjacent areas of the city). Not contested (§6.4): the letter offers no reanalysis of the study's areas and does not change the reading of the claim as worded, an unadjusted association near one site. Also read against the letter's other source on heroin, which the study itself cites too (Wood et al., 2006, dated 2004 in the letter), from its PDF: rating and status unchanged. It is a comparison of periods by three of the study's authors (card sc_wood_2006, ROBINS-E high): it measured no heroin purity, price or availability directly, has no figures after 2003 (2004 for its cohort) and none for the study's two areas, so it tests neither the letter's explanation nor the study's association. Its yearly figures fill in the background. Across British Columbia, overdose deaths fell mostly from 1998 to 2000, were about level in 2001 and lower in 2002 and 2003, which partly fits the letter's point that 2001 had more deaths than later years, but places most of the fall before the study began; the paper itself counts 2001 in the period of reduced supply, and in its figures 2001 was about level with 2000 for deaths and about half of 2000 for seizures, so it shows 2001 neither as clearly high nor as clearly low. Ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside fell in every fiscal year to 2002–03, a fall under way in the site's neighbourhood during the before period that the study's unadjusted two-period comparison cannot separate from the opening, although whether the rest of the city fell alike is not shown. Self-reported daily heroin injection in the team's cohort was lower in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000. The paper does not contain the figures the study cites it for (daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting 17% and 15%, stable methadone use), which leaves the study's statement that drug use stayed constant without a source that can be checked here; the reply's sources for the same point are other reports, not on file. These points add to the reasons for the existing risk-of-bias downgrade rather than changing it, and the rating is already very low. Later evaluations of the same site, on the project's PDF request list, are not on file; the claim must still be read against them before it leaves draft (METHODS §2.3).
rate.population: Residents of the City of Vancouver as the denominator (census populations; on average about 8,100 before and 8,800 after within 500 metres of the site, editors' calculation from person-years), with the 290 deaths ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses by the British Columbia Coroners Service from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2005 (229 men; median age 40), counted by place of death; the site's neighbourhood, the Downtown Eastside, had about 5,000 people who inject drugs, as cited
rate.exposure: Place of death within 500 metres of North America's first medically supervised injection site (all census blocks whose centre lay within 500 metres, fixed in advance because over 70% of daily clients in a random sample lived within that distance), after its opening on 21 September 2003 (to 31 December 2005); no individual measure of use of the site
rate.comparator: The same area before the opening (1 January 2001 to 20 September 2003), and the rest of the city over the same two periods; no adjustment for other factors
rate.outcome: Rate of coroner-ruled accidental illicit drug overdose deaths per 100,000 person-years (census populations interpolated between 2001 and 2006), compared as rate differences and percentage falls, with a Breslow-Day test of the difference between areas
rate.magnitude: Marshall et al. (2011), Table 2: within 500 m, 56 deaths over 22,066 person-years (253.8 per 100,000; 95% CI 187.3 to 320.3) before and 33 over 19,991 (165.1; 108.8 to 221.4) after; rate difference 88.7 (1.6 to 175.8), p=0.048; fall 35.0% (0.0% to 57.7%). Rest of city: 113 over 1,479,792 (7.6; 6.2 to 9.0) and 88 over 1,271,246 (6.9; 5.5 to 8.4); rate difference 0.7 (−1.3 to 2.7), p=0.490; fall 9.3% (−19.8% to 31.4%). Breslow-Day test of the rate differences p=0.049. Population held at its 2001 level: fall 30% within 500 m, not significant (no interval). Blocks: 15 of 22 fell, Wilcoxon p=0.039 (also with the population held fixed). Editors' calculation: about 20.6 deaths a year before and 14.5 after within 500 m (about 6 fewer a year), and 41.5 and 38.6 elsewhere; rate ratio 0.65 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.00) within 500 m and 0.91 (0.69 to 1.20) elsewhere, not significantly different (p about 0.20). Authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012, p. 118): restricted to deaths with indirect signs of injection (85% of the 89 within 500 m; about 76, editors' calculation), the fall within 500 m was 36%, with no count, rates, interval, p value or result for the rest of the city. The letter (Christian et al., 2012, p. 117) gives no estimate for the study's areas: its figure plots yearly counts, not rates, for British Columbia, Vancouver and the Downtown Eastside (editors' reading, approximate: Vancouver about 89, 49, 49, 66 and 56 deaths in 2001–2005; the Downtown Eastside about 31, 27, 29, 32 and 37). Cited papers on file: Kerr et al. (2007, p. 40 and Fig. 1), in a cohort of 1,587 people who inject drugs (12,030 interviews, 1996–2004), the yearly share reporting a non-fatal overdose in the previous 6 months was 21% in 1997 and 6% in 2004 (text); editors' reading of the figure, approximate: about 12% in 2001, 5% in 2002, 7% in 2003 and 6% in 2004; yearly denominators not printed. Wood et al. (2004, p. 1554), police crackdown from 7 April 2003: used syringes found discarded in public, monthly averages for January–March against April–June 2003, 1,082 to 585 within a block of Main and Hastings and 784 to 1,253 in the rest of the Downtown Eastside (counted only there); no overdose data. Wood et al. (2006; Table 1, p. 691; Figure 1, p. 692; Table 2, p. 693): yearly averages, overdose deaths in British Columbia 297 (1998–2000) and 192 (2001–03), 35.4% lower; naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside 674 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01) and 370 (2001–02 to 2002–03), 45.1% lower; heroin seized for Canada 184 and 67 kg, 63.6% lower; no tests. Editors' reading of Figure 1 (approximate): deaths about 399, 272, 218, 221, 169 and 186 (1998–2003); naloxone-requiring responses about 732, 840, 655, 464, 388 and 350 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2002–03); heroin seized about 234, 142, 177, 94, 46 and 60 kg (1998–2003); period means within 1 of Table 1. Cohort: daily heroin injection, adjusted odds ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.61) for 2001–04 against 1996–2000; 36.5%, 32.6%, 23.3% and 20.8% in 1997/98, 1999/00, 2001/02 and 2003/04; no figures for 2005.
rate.short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.
rate.rate: One before-and-after study of one site in Vancouver, allowing for nothing else that changed, like policing or a fall in overdoses already under way. With few deaths, the drop was barely bigger than chance.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_moss_2017 (editors' narrative-review checklist): overall high. The evidence was chosen by a task force after a literature search with no stated databases, dates, terms or criteria; the recommendations are, in the statement's own words, primarily consensus expert opinion; the absence of poisoned responders is the authors' observation, without a search record, a case series or a count of exposures; the incidents are represented by a DEA warning and news reports and are not examined one by one. Card sc_herman_2020 (JBI prevalence checklist, first pass): moderate for what the count describes, whether news articles reported a confirmed exposure: each article coded by one reviewer against undefined criteria, with no agreement statistic, distinct incidents not counted, and results given only for the three-part combination. Card sc_niosh_2018 (JBI checklist, first pass): high for any conclusion about cause: no biological, air or skin sample, a field test contradicted by the laboratory, no record of which item formed the cloud of powder, and an account reconstructed four months later. Card sc_chiu_2019 (JBI checklist, first pass): high for any conclusion about cause: two referred incidents chosen to illustrate scenarios, reconstructed weeks to months later, with nothing measured on the officers or around them and no test able to detect fentanyl. All four share one gap, the absence of any measurement of exposure, so one level, not two.

inconsistency.note: None: the position statement (from its authors' knowledge), the news review and the three incidents investigated by NIOSH all report no confirmed case; they differ in design and none estimates a rate.

indirectness.note: Second-hand and extrapolated in the position statement: the skin estimate uses fentanyl patch data, a steady-state rate through a matrix designed to deliver the drug, which the authors themselves say overstates uptake from powder or tablets; the air estimate uses industrial exposure data whose inputs are not given; both are for fentanyl only, with no figure for carfentanil or other analogues; the 100-microgram reference amount is not explained; and the statement concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. The news review examined news text, not medical, police or laboratory records. In the NIOSH incident the powder reached the officers' faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and no opioid was identified in the seized items, so it bears on reported exposures in general, not on skin contact with fentanyl. In the first incident of Chiu et al. the powder, which contained methamphetamine as well as fentanyl, blew onto the officer and the uniform outdoors in wind, so breathing it in or contact with the eyes, nose or mouth are not excluded; in the second the officers were in or near a room with scattered powders and residues; neither bears on skin contact alone.

imprecision.note: Not rated separately: no source estimates a rate or count of poisonings among exposed responders (the news review counts articles, not exposures or incidents, and the three investigated incidents have no denominator), a gap already counted under risk of bias; very low is the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. The news review describes the media's own selection (incidents that reached English-language news indexed by LexisNexis); that selection is counted under risk of bias and indirectness, not here.

rate.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November with the first data on file, a review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020) and a NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation (Jackson et al., 2018), both read from their PDFs. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review, but its certainty stays very low and its relation insufficient evidence. All four sources are observational, so the start is low (METHODS §6.3): the news review is a case series of media-reported incidents, the evaluation a single case report, Chiu et al. a case series of two further incidents, and the position statement, filed as a narrative review, starts from the design of what it describes (pharmacokinetic studies of fentanyl patches and of inhaled fentanyl, a patch product label, industrial exposure limits, one small volunteer study, one case report, one animal study and agency warnings, none randomized and none a study of exposed responders). Down one level for risk of bias: the statement's unsystematic selection and consensus opinion, the news review's undefined criteria applied by one reviewer per article with incidents not counted, and the evaluation's reconstruction from records and interviews four months later with nothing measured; all four share one gap, the absence of any measurement of exposure, so one level, not two. Down one for indirectness: patch and industrial data applied to powder on the skin (fentanyl only), news text instead of medical, police or laboratory records, and one incident in which the powder reached the officers' faces and no opioid was found in the seized items: very low, the floor, so imprecision (no source can give a rate) is not counted again. Inconsistency is now assessable and absent: none of the four reports a confirmed case. The new data do not raise the rating because both are descriptive records with no denominator of exposures: the news review's zero follows mainly from testing almost never being mentioned (one incident, two articles), so it shows that the news did not report confirmation, not that no responder was poisoned; and the evaluation tested neither officer, so it can neither confirm nor exclude poisoning in that incident, while its laboratory found no opioid in what was seized. Companion paper of 13 November: Chiu et al. (2019), NIOSH's account of two further incidents with five officers, read as its author manuscript, adds no confirmed case and no measurement, and does not change the rating: the officer onto whom powder later found to contain fentanyl with methamphetamine was blown had non-specific symptoms within 5 minutes, no recorded sign of opioid toxicity and no laboratory test; in the other incident the urine screens, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative, and the authors' reading of one officer's rapid improvement after naloxone as a sign of opioid involvement rests on one uncontrolled observation. Its incidents are not the one in the NIOSH report (other evaluation numbers, other details), but two of its authors wrote that report. The relation stays insufficient evidence: no source measured exposure, so neither poisoning from skin contact nor its absence can be shown with any precision, and none could have detected how often poisoning happens. The societies' judgment that the risk is extremely low and that skin absorption is unlikely, or very unlikely, to cause toxicity is reported as their judgment, with their own hedges (unlikely, very unlikely, likely to give reasonable protection), and NIOSH's statement on brief skin contact as NIOSH's own position, which cites the societies' statement among its sources; neither is adopted as the editors' finding. Where the statement's summary is firmer than the section it summarizes (an N95 gives sufficient protection, against an N95 or P100 likely to give reasonable protection), both are given. The single quotation records the statement's own description of its basis. Not used: the statement's naloxone section and NIOSH's recommendations, in the 2018 report and in Chiu et al. (guidance, which this answer does not cover), the second-hand figures on deaths from synthetic opioids, and the news review's untested suggestions (a nocebo effect; protective equipment delaying care). Status replicated, for the absence of a confirmed case only (METHODS §6.4): two independent primary studies of different design, the news review (by a Johns Hopkins team whose senior author is the position statement's last author) and the NIOSH evaluation, agree that no confirmed opioid poisoning was documented, as the statement says from its authors' knowledge; none measured exposure, and none can show that no responder was ever poisoned. Chiu et al. agree, but they share two authors with the NIOSH evaluation and are not counted as a third independent study. The four anchors from Chiu et al. (16 to 19) are ai-located and await a second reader's check.
rate.population: Emergency responders (law enforcement and emergency medical services) in North America who may meet fentanyl or fentanyl analogues as powder, tablets or liquid on calls, at crime scenes or in drug raids: as considered in a 2017 position statement, which studied no responders, exposures or cases; as reported in 214 English-language North American news articles (January 2012 to March 2018) that described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid; and two sheriff's department officers in one incident in early 2018, investigated afterwards by NIOSH, and five police officers in two other incidents of 2017 and 2018, also investigated afterwards by NIOSH (Chiu et al., 2019)
rate.exposure: Incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues: on the skin (the question here), and also airborne powder breathed in, splashes to the eyes or mouth, and being near the drug; reasoned from pharmacokinetic data in the position statement, as reported in news articles (routes recorded but not reported), and, in the NIOSH incident, white powder of unknown composition blown into two officers' faces; in the two incidents of Chiu et al., powder blown onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, which the laboratory later found to contain fentanyl with methamphetamine, and a hotel room with drug powders in view, with items from it handled elsewhere; no source measured any exposure
rate.comparator: None in any source: the position statement collected no data, and its worked arithmetic takes as its reference the time needed to absorb 100 micrograms of fentanyl through the skin, or the exposure needed to reach a dose of 100 micrograms from the air, an amount it does not justify; the news review and the incident investigations had no comparison group
rate.outcome: Clinically significant opioid toxicity in the responder (objective signs such as slowed breathing or a lowered level of consciousness), as distinct from nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness or anxiety; in the news review, a confirmed exposure (an article describing a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together); in the NIOSH incidents, symptoms and clinical findings in emergency medical service and emergency department records (with urine drug screens, unable to detect fentanyl, in four officers), and forensic analysis of the substances seized
rate.magnitude: No measured rate or count of poisonings. ACMT and AACT position (Moss et al., 2017): risk of clinically significant exposure extremely low; no reports seen of responders with signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact; incidental skin absorption unlikely (summary) or very unlikely (recommendations) to cause toxicity. Worked arithmetic, fentanyl only: both palms covered by fentanyl patches (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%, delivery 2.5 micrograms per cm2 per hour at steady state), about 14 minutes to absorb 100 micrograms (editors' check: 170 cm2 × 2.5 = 425 micrograms an hour, so 14.1 minutes); patches take 3–13 hours to give a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 hours to peak; at the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed); vapour pressure 4.6 × 10^-6 Pa. Mucous membranes: more than 30-fold the absorption of skin; one case report of drowsiness after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, its cause unclear to the authors. No estimate for carfentanil (10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals) or any other analogue. Respiratory protection: an N95 respirator or P100 mask likely to give reasonable protection against significant airborne powder (recommendations); an N95 sufficient in exceptional circumstances with particles or droplets in the air (summary). Herman et al. (2020), English-language North American print and online news (LexisNexis), January 2012 to March 2018: 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 relevant (editors: 72%), 214 describing a specific responder exposure (editors: 21% of relevant); 0 of 214 with a plausible route, consistent symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing together; any laboratory testing of an exposed person mentioned for 1 incident (2 articles; editors: 0.9% of 214), an opiate urine result; distinct incidents not counted, and no count reported for any single criterion. Jackson et al. (2018; NIOSH), 1 incident, 2 officers: no laboratory test of either officer; no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity in EMS or emergency department records (alert and oriented, normal oxygen saturation, normal-sized pupils, normal heart and respiratory rates in the emergency department, blood pressure raised); observed for more than an hour and discharged; naloxone given to one officer at the scene; seized items: cocaine, methamphetamine and THC identified, alprazolam and sodium bicarbonate only indicated, no fentanyl or other opioid, against a presumptive field result for fentanyl; no exposure measured. Chiu et al. (2019; NIOSH), 2 incidents, 5 officers: no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl (HHE 1, no laboratory test; HHE 2, urine screens negative for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates, with cut-offs of 500 ng/mL for amphetamines and 150 ng/mL for cocaine; opiate screens do not detect fentanyl); HHE 1: onset within 5 minutes; first vital signs blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17, heart rate 105, pupils 4 mm and reactive; later heart rate 80–85, breathing rate 15–21, blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104; powder left in the container 1.56 g, fentanyl and methamphetamine identified; HHE 2: onset about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began for the three officers who entered the room and about 30 to 45 minutes after handling items for the fourth; one dose of intranasal naloxone to one officer, with rapid improvement; no depressed breathing reported; one breathing rate of 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department; hotel-room evidence: fentanyl 0.14 g, heroin 0.14 g, N-ethylpentylone 2.87 g, para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl, dibutylone, and cocaine and methamphetamine residues; no exposure measured; perceived risk not assessed.
rate.short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.
rate.rate: Expert sums from skin patches, 214 news stories and three incidents a safety agency looked into; nobody measured real touches. Finding no proven case can't show how often, if ever, it happens.

risk_of_bias.note: Rated for the claim as worded, a description of what was answered and said. Coverage and response: attendees of trainings, not samples drawn at random (Missouri: 140 of 200 analysed, 43 unexplained; Indiana: 129 of 204 at baseline and 69 at follow-up); interviewees picked by agency contacts at purposively chosen agencies, 3 of the 23 not asked; New York: 187 self-selected respondents reached through 3 of 15 associations, flyers and personal contacts, with no knowable response rate. Measurement: single unvalidated items, the Indiana one combining touching with inhaling and asking about great risk, the New York one reported only as agree or disagree; second answers given right after the corrective message by people who knew the intended answer; interview themes reported without counts. Cards (first pass): sc_winograd_2020 and sc_del_pozo_2021 critical under ROBINS-I as estimates of a training effect, which this claim does not make; sc_attaway_2021 some concerns; sc_beletsky_2020 moderate, with a misinformation category that includes neutral incident reports and reach figures that are upper bounds; sc_persaud_2020 high under the JBI checklist (first pass), with no sampling frame or response rate. One level: these problems could change the figures materially but not their direction.

inconsistency.note: None: the three survey baselines agree (about 4 in 5) despite different items, states and years, the interviews agree without counts, and both before-and-after comparisons move the same way.

indirectness.note: Attendees of overdose-response and harm-reduction trainings in two Midwestern states in 2019 to 2021, self-selected New York State responders in 2019, and five agencies in 2020: how far they represent US police generally, or beliefs today, is unknown. The Missouri and Indiana items ask about overdose and the New York item about death, and the Indiana item combines touching with inhaling. The second answers measure what people said right after a lesson, not lasting belief or behaviour at overdose scenes. The news study counts online articles and Facebook shares, not what officers saw or believed.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: the baseline intervals are moderately narrow (Indiana agreement about 72% to 86%; Missouri answering False about 15% to 28%; New York agreement about 73% to 85%, editors' calculation); the Indiana follow-up rests on 69 people (about 28% to 51%), an uncertainty smaller than that from the missing two-thirds, which is counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: two evaluations, each by a team that developed or delivers the training it evaluated, with no registration; an unpublished evaluation that found no change cannot be excluded, but none is known.

rate.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3): it reports how many responders said they held the belief, where they said it came from, how news coverage carried it, and how answers differed just after a training; it does not claim that training changed beliefs, which these designs cannot show. Descriptive, observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias (training attendees and a self-selected online sample rather than random samples, heavy missing data, single unvalidated items, second answers given straight after the corrective message, interviews without counts) and one for indirectness (two Midwestern states, New York State and five agencies in 2019 to 2021; items about overdose, and in New York about death, one combining touching with inhaling; answers rather than behaviour): very low. Not upgraded: descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect, and the before-and-after shifts are not estimates of an effect. Rated as worded: as estimates of a training effect, both training studies are at critical risk of bias under ROBINS-I (no comparison group, an immediate post-test, attrition), so a claim that training changes the belief would also be very low, and the statement says that the designs cannot show it. The single quotation records the Missouri item itself, because its wording is the measure; the Indiana item, 17 words long, is paraphrased. Editors' calculations (Wilson intervals; counts from the printed group percentages; the recomputed standardized effects, d about 0.40 and 0.56 and d_z about 0.78; the interval for the paired change; the ratios of shares) are labelled for the second reader to recompute. Printed figures corrected or qualified: the Missouri overall 20.9% fits 29 of 139, not of 140 (20.7%), and its differences are percentage points; the Indiana Cohen's d values (2.33, 1.61, 2.33) are incompatible with the printed t and group sizes, its paired interval matches d_z rather than the mean change, and its printed patrol means contradict the stated direction; the Indiana abstract's 79.8% against 39.1% mixes denominators of 129 and 69 and calls a 3-hour training with a 10-minute module a 10-minute online training; the news study's 6.6% of total is 6.6% of misinformation shares (6.0% of all), and its 70 million people reached are an upper bound on views; and the interview study's abstract says more than its Results. Beliefs are reported as beliefs: the papers' description of the belief as false rests on the 2017 ACMT and AACT position statement and similar sources, and this project rates that question separately (very low certainty, insufficient evidence, no confirmed case on file), so the answer says what people believed, not whether they were right. Status replicated (METHODS §6.4), for the share holding the belief: the New York survey (Persaud & Jennings, 2020), which shares no author with the others, finds about 4 in 5 agreeing that a brief touch could be deadly, as the two training surveys find for overdose; those two share two authors (Goulka, Beletsky), and Beletsky is also first author of the news study; the interview study shares no author with them (one of its authors and Beletsky list the same University of California, San Diego division) and agrees that concern was near universal among those asked, but without counts it cannot replicate the figures. Companion paper of 13 November: the New York survey, cited second-hand through Attaway et al. (nearly 80%) in the earlier version, is now read first-hand (Persaud & Jennings, 2020): its 79.7% is agreement, at levels it does not report, in a self-selected sample; it adds a third state, a statement about death rather than overdose, and the only counts of information sources on file, which it did not link to the belief. The four anchors added on 13 November (12 to 15) and the reworded anchor 8 await a second reader's check, and card sc_persaud_2020 its round-2 reading.

rate.short: In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death. Right after trainings, far fewer did.
rate.rate: Three surveys in three US states, none picking people at random, two of them at trainings by partly the same researchers, plus interviews. Answers after training came at once, with no untrained group.

risk_of_bias.note: Primary studies read in full: Tjio et al. (1969), coded samples scored blind before and after one dose, but no untreated comparison group, other medicines in 31 of 32 patients and infections between samples (card sc_tjio_1969, ROBINS-I serious); Irwin and Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967), cross-sectional comparisons that found more breaks (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12), with coded slides but no samples from before LSD, recruitment not described, self-reported LSD of unstated source and no statistical comparison; the first with groups differing in sex and x-ray exposure and other hallucinogens uncounted (ROBINS-E high), the second with other drugs or medicines in every LSD patient, similar rates in its own patients taking other drugs without LSD and two controls with high rates left out after the fact (ROBINS-E very high); Loughman et al. (1967) and Sparkes et al. (1968), cross-sectional comparisons that found none, of 8 people against 19 controls and of 4 against 4, with groups differing in other drugs, age and psychiatric illness, illicit exposure self-reported and blinding of the scorers not reported in Sparkes et al. (ROBINS-E high); Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors with no statistical test, and one patient without a sample from before LSD (editors' checklist, high). The later studies that reported raised breakage in groups of people are known only through the narrative review (card sc_dishotsky_1971: no search method or selection criteria; unpublished data, including the authors' own; its second author led Loughman et al., 1967) and cannot be appraised; as the review describes them they were small, with nearly universal use of other drugs, laboratories differing in methods, thresholds and control rates (0% to 11.9%), and no account of whether scorers knew which samples were exposed; one widely deviant value was excluded from a negative group.

inconsistency.note: Three teams reported raised breakage in people who used LSD and many other drugs, two of them in first reports now read in full (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), and LSD given into a vein raised it for a time in 3 people (as the review describes it), whereas the other studies read in full found no excess (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969, with 3 large rises among 32 patients), and most other teams in the review found none either. The explanation offered (other drugs and medicines, contaminated street drugs, infections, malnutrition, culture methods and high control rates) is plausible, and one paper read first-hand bears it out in part: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had rates similar to 18 LSD patients (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); but that comparison rests on 6 people, mostly taking prescribed medicines, and the rest on the review's account and its authors' impressions.

indirectness.note: Breaks seen under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture stand in for genetic harm in people; blood cells are not sperm or egg cells, which none of these studies examined (Tjio et al., 1969, p. 855); the cell studies (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967, and part of Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967) are not studies of people; children exposed before birth were compared with adults; hospital patients given pharmaceutical LSD, nearly all after other medicines, differ from people taking street LSD of unknown content; methods of 1967 to 1970; apart from the first two, the studies that reported raised breakage in people are seen only second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: Groups of 4 to 32 people in the primary studies read (1 to 46 in the review); in the largest study the 95% interval of the change, about −1.3 to +4.6 points from a starting 4.28% (editors' calculation from Tjio et al.'s Table 2), includes no change and a rise to about double; with 4 people per group only groups that do not overlap at all can differ significantly (Sparkes et al., 1968); the two studies that found an excess compared 8 with 9 and 18 with 12 people and reported no test (editors' 95% intervals of the differences 3.7 to 19.7 and 6.2 to 12.3 breaks per 100 cells), and the comparison that could separate LSD from other drugs rests on 6 people (interval of the difference −7.3 to 6.1); the review's counts have no intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review itself includes unpublished data.

rate.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November because four of the primary studies had been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3); later that day the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage were read in full too (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), without a change of rating. The human primary studies are observational, four cross-sectional comparisons and one before-and-after study without an untreated group, and start low; the cell-culture studies are preclinical and can only be indirect for people (§5.4). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision (domain notes): very low, the floor; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down twice, with the same result. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither an increase in breakage after LSD nor its absence can be shown with precision (§6.1): in the strongest study the share of cells with aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not significantly, with a 95% interval of the change (about −1.3 to +4.6 points, editors' calculation) that includes no change and a rise to about double, and 3 of 32 patients had large rises, back within the normal range in the 2 retested; the two cross-sectional studies that found no excess (8 people; groups of 4) cannot exclude a modest rise; the two that found about two and three times the controls' break rates (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12) had no samples from before LSD, did not describe recruitment and reported no statistical comparison, and in the larger of them every LSD patient had taken other drugs or medicines and 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so the excess cannot be attributed to LSD; and the cell studies reported no statistical test and no consistent concentration–response. Of the human studies that reported raised breakage, Irwin & Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) are now read in full; they leave the inconsistency and risk-of-bias judgments as they were, with the explanation of the positive findings now resting partly on first-hand data. The study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968) and the two laboratories' later studies enter only as the review describes them. The review is not independent of one negative study: its second author was the first author of Loughman et al. (1967), and its tables include the authors' own unpublished study. Where the review's figures differ from the primary papers, the primary papers are used: Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients and 5 volunteers, not 37 patients; one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate; the 5 volunteers' final average is 3.17% in the paper's own Table 4, not the printed 3.57% (editors' calculation); Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s cell study, which the review lists as significant, reports no test; Irwin and Egozcue print no group means, and their table gives 23.6 and 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation), not the review's 23.4% and 11.0% (11.9% in its table); Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say where their patients' LSD came from, report no test for their cells in a dish, and their Table 5 sums to 7735 treated cells, not 8725; and the review's statement that no positive study showed a relation with dose does not fit Irwin and Egozcue's own table, in which the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate in 8 people (editors' calculation). Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say whether their case 37, who matches Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s single patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, is the same man; if so, the review counts him both among people given pharmaceutical LSD and among people exposed to illicit LSD. The claim reports what was measured and where raised breakage was seen, so that a reader can see that the early reports came from people using many drugs and medicines and were not confirmed by the other teams; it does not adopt the review's closing statement that the authors believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man, which goes beyond the review's own findings that no significant work on cancer had been reported and that the human data on birth defects were case reports and one series. The cross-study tallies (14.29% against 48.9%) compare different laboratories and criteria and are not used as a rate ratio. Fly and animal findings are labelled and not used for people. Status mixed: the studies disagree, and the explanation offered for the positive findings (other drugs and medicines, street-drug contents, infections, culture methods) is plausible, and supported in one study by a small comparison group, but not established. The new anchors are not yet checked by a second reader, and studies after 1970 were not read and could change the claim. The statement gives no doses.
rate.population: People whose blood cells were examined from 1967 to 1970. Read in full: cultured white blood cells from two donors and one man treated with LSD in psychotherapy (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967); 8 men reporting LSD use against 9 volunteers without it (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967); 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD, 12 drug-free controls (2 more left out), 4 children exposed before birth and cultured cells from 6 donors (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use against 19 laboratory controls (Loughman et al., 1967); three groups of 4, namely hospital volunteers, psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and patients given LSD in treatment (Sparkes et al., 1968); and 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before (Tjio et al., 1969). As summarized in one narrative review: 21 reports from 17 laboratories with 310 people, 126 given pharmaceutical (pure) LSD in medical or research settings (many of them patients, some treated with psychiatric medicines) and 184 who had used illicit drugs sold as LSD (nearly all of whom also used other drugs), in groups of 1 to 46 people, 56 of the 126 tested before and after LSD; children exposed before birth reported separately (14 exposed to illicit LSD); also cultured cells, fruit flies, a fungus, rodents and monkeys
rate.exposure: Pharmaceutical LSD given under supervision (one to three treatments in the before-and-after studies, by mouth except in one study of 3 people given it into a vein; more in some comparison studies, for example 15 sessions in Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient), or self-reported use of LSD outside medical settings, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, of unknown content and strength (the source is not stated in Irwin & Egozcue, 1967, or Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); in laboratory studies, LSD added to cultured cells
rate.comparator: Unexposed control groups (breakage rates of 0% to 11.9% between laboratories), each person's own sample from before LSD (with no untreated group sampled at the same times in the largest study), untreated cultures in the cell studies, or, in one study, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967)
rate.outcome: Chromosome breakage, mostly chromatid-type breaks, counted under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture (as breaks per cell or as the share of cells with an aberration, which differ between studies); also, as reported in the review, case reports of cancer, birth defects and spontaneous abortions after LSD, mutations in fruit flies and a fungus, and malformations in rodents and monkeys
rate.magnitude: Primary studies read in full. Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors: 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 LSD conditions against 0.037 (34 of 925 cells) in untreated cultures, no statistical test (384 breaks in 2678 treated cells, 0.143 per cell, editors' sum); one patient 12% in 200 cells, no sample from before LSD. Irwin & Egozcue (1967): breaks per 100 cells 12.0 to 38.0 in 8 men reporting LSD use against 7.0 to 25.0 in 9 volunteers without it; means 23.6 against 11.9 (378 of 1600 and 215 of 1800 cells; difference 11.7, 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7, editors' calculation; the review prints 23.4% against 11.0% in its text and 11.9% in its table); P < .05 for 6 of 8 and 1 of 9 people, test not named. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967): 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 drug-free controls, no test (difference 9.3, 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3, editors' calculation; with the 2 controls left out after a viral illness included, 5.4 pooled (161 in 2974) and a per-person mean of 6.5, a difference in per-person means of 6.6, 1.5 to 11.7); 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD 12.6 (mean of six rates; 161 in 1361 cells), not different from the LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84, editors' calculation); 4 children exposed before birth 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults; cells in a dish from 6 donors 7.7 to 17.5 against 3.9 (1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells, editors' sum; the review lists 8725 cells), no concentration-response, no test. Loughman et al. (1967): 0 chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people (95% limits 0.0% to 0.5%) against 0 of 112 (1 concurrent control), 1 of 561 (0.2%; 18 earlier controls) and 11 of 1569 (0.7%; published controls), not significant. Sparkes et al. (1968): breaks per 100 cells 2.2 (21/937; LSD taken privately, 4 people), 1.5 (14/914; LSD in treatment, 4) and 1.6 (15/950; controls, 4); cells with a break 1.4%, 1.4% and 1.5%; not significant (with 4 against 4 the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.029, editors' calculation). Tjio et al. (1969), 32 patients before and after one dose: cells with aberrations 4.28% to 5.91% (+1.63 points; P = 0.3; lower dose level, 11 patients, 4.05% to 9.26%, P = 0.15; higher, 21 patients, 4.39% to 4.16%, P = 0.8); editors' calculation: 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 points, 18 rose, 12 fell, 2 unchanged; 3 rises of more than 4 points (2.44% to 23.08%, 9.50% to 43.92%, 1.48% to 14.16%), 2 retested at 4.76% (71 days) and 1.48% (229 days); 5 volunteers with earlier illicit use 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from Table 4, editors' calculation), not significant. Dishotsky et al. (1971), counts without intervals: breakage above control means in at most 18 of 126 people given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%; 45.98%, 80 of 174, without one study's incomplete data); 18 of the 108 people reported with damage had pharmaceutical LSD (16.67%). Illicit-LSD studies: 80 of 86 raised in two early teams' studies (for example 18.76% against 9.03% in 46 people, and 13.2% against 3.8% in 18); none beyond the general population in nine other teams' studies (88 people, editors' sum). Pharmaceutical LSD compared with unexposed controls: at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), as few as 3 of 61 (4.9%). Before and after: 6 of 56 raised (10.7%); group averages 5.7% to 4.9% (10 people), 0.0% to 0.0% (6), 2.81% to 3.57% (5) and 4.28% to 5.91% (32), not significant; 1.0% to 4.78% after intravenous LSD (3 people), significant; 50 of 53 given LSD by mouth (94.3%) showed no increase. Other drugs: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD 12.6% against 13.2% in 18 patients with LSD and other drugs, not significantly different by the review's own comparison (the paper reports none; editors' check above). In vitro: 6 of 9 studies positive; in one study LSD 10.2%, aspirin 9.6% and ergonovine 10.0% against 5.0% in control cells. Pregnancies: spontaneous abortion 37% (pharmaceutical plus illicit LSD), 15% (pharmaceutical only), 20% (general population), in 148 pregnancies with 12 exposed during gestation.
rate.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
rate.rate: Small, old studies of blood cells under a microscope. The best had no group without LSD, the studies disagree, and those that found more damage could not tell LSD apart from other drugs.

item.statement: In a UK expert ranking, alcohol came top mostly because of the harm it does to other people.
item.why: 46 of its 72 points were harm to others. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worse.

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.

Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

item.statement: A study proved that Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs cut overdose deaths nearby.
item.why: Not proven: deaths nearby fell more than elsewhere, but nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.

lines.short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.
lines.but: Just one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.
how: Coroners recorded 290 overdose deaths from illegal drugs in Vancouver, 2001 to 2005. About half involved opioids, and about 6 in 10 cocaine.
Within 500 metres: 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before it opened in 2003, 33 in the 2.3 after, about 6 fewer a year.
Critics blamed extra police from April 2003. The authors said that crackdown ended within weeks of the opening.
Critics also blamed more heroin in 2001. Their two papers show overdoses falling since the late 1990s, and more in 2001 than in 2002, but neither measured how strong heroin was or what it cost.

item.statement: Overdoses were already falling years before Vancouver's injection site opened.
item.why: In the two papers critics cited, overdoses fell from the late 1990s on, and the site opened in 2003.

item.statement: Poison experts say fentanyl splashed into the eyes or mouth is no real risk.
item.why: They treat splashes into the eyes or mouth as a real risk, unlike a brief touch on the skin, which they call very unlikely to poison.

lines.short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.
lines.but: Nobody has measured real touches, and finding no proven case is not proof it never happens.
how: Poison experts worked out that palms covered in fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver it, would need about 14 minutes to pass a high dose.
Researchers checked 214 news stories about police or paramedics exposed to opioids. Only one incident mentioned any test, probably one that misses fentanyl.
A federal safety agency looked into three cases where seven officers felt ill. It found no signs of a serious overdose. No officer had a test that finds fentanyl.
Splashes into the eyes or mouth are treated as a real risk. No sums were done for carfentanil, far stronger than morphine in animals.

lines.statement: In the City of Vancouver, Canada, in 2001–2005, the opening of North America's first medically supervised injection site (the supervised injecting facility in the Downtown Eastside, opened on 21 September 2003, where people inject drugs obtained beforehand under the supervision of health professionals who give emergency care, including oxygen and naloxone; by an earlier count, heroin made up about 40% of the injections there, powder cocaine about 30% and methamphetamine 5%) is associated with a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 metres of the site than in the rest of the city, in one before-and-after study without adjustment for anything else. Within 500 metres there were 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before the opening (22,066 person-years; 253.8 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI 187.3 to 320.3) and 33 in the 2.3 years after (19,991 person-years; 165.1, 108.8 to 221.4), a fall of 35.0% (0.0% to 57.7%; rate difference 88.7 per 100,000 person-years, 1.6 to 175.8, p=0.048), about 6 fewer deaths a year (editors' calculation: about 20.6 a year before and 14.5 after); in the rest of the city there were 113 deaths (1,479,792 person-years; 7.6 per 100,000) and 88 (1,271,246; 6.9), a fall of 9.3% (−19.8% to 31.4%; p=0.490). The test of the difference between the two falls in absolute terms (rate differences; Breslow-Day) gave p=0.049, which the summary calls a significant interaction and the results describe as heterogeneity that might be present; the relative falls (rate ratios 0.65 and 0.91) do not differ significantly (p about 0.20; editors' calculations). The rates rest on census populations interpolated between 2001 and 2006: the population of city blocks within 500 metres rose 14% from 2001 to 2005, which the authors link to more supportive housing, and with the population held at its 2001 level the fall near the site was 30% and not statistically significant (no interval or p value given), although a block-by-block test still showed an overall fall with either population (15 of 22 blocks with deaths fell; p=0.039 both ways). In census tracts, falls were larger nearer the site, minimal beyond about 500 metres and negligible beyond 1 km. Deaths were counted by the place of death, not by use of the site, and no individual was followed (Marshall et al., 2011, a retrospective population-based study of all 290 deaths ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses by the British Columbia Coroners Service, 89 of them, 30.7%, within 500 metres and 201 farther away). The coroners recorded opioids as contributing to 156 of the 290 deaths and cocaine to 175 (editors' sums from Table 1; a death can involve both), with no significant change in the drugs involved in either area; the paper does not mention fentanyl. The authors could not adjust for neighbourhood changes because Statistics Canada suppressed area characteristics; they report no evidence of changes in drug supply or purity, drug-use patterns, methadone treatment, policing or migration, partly from other studies; one spike of deaths from stolen powdered methadone, after the opening; and police referral of people injecting in public to the site throughout; they state that confounding by unmeasured factors cannot be excluded and that the area-level design calls for caution. High overdose mortality in Vancouver in the 1990s led to the site's opening in the Downtown Eastside; it had 12 injection seats, over 500 supervised injections a day and about 5,000 people who inject drugs nearby, and an earlier study had recorded no deaths inside it. The authors (funded by Vancouver Coastal Health, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research; three of the five also wrote earlier reports of the site's evaluation, which was first funded by Health Canada) call such facilities safe and effective in the discussion, and conclude that they should be considered for assessment where injection drug use is prevalent. A published letter (Christian et al., 2012) argues that the decline owes much to starting in 2001, a year in which, it says, heroin was far more available and deaths more common than in any later year, and that police added in 2003 to 12 city blocks around the site, where it says most of the deaths behind the fall lay (48 to 66 officers, still deployed when it wrote, by an unnamed personal communication), are the most likely cause of any real fall; its own data are yearly death counts, not rates, plotted without values for British Columbia, Vancouver and the Downtown Eastside, all larger areas than the study's (editors' reading of the plot, approximate: Vancouver about 89 deaths in 2001, 49 in 2002 and 56 in 2005; the Downtown Eastside about 31, 27 and 37 in the same years). None of the three papers it cites on heroin and policing, all now on file, measured heroin purity or availability directly (Kerr et al., 2007, and Wood et al., 2006, which it dates 2004, cited for the 2001 point; Wood et al., 2004, cited for policing). The authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012) answers that the letter's Downtown Eastside figures cover the whole local health area (about 400 city blocks, against the study's 41) and, by its account, all drug-induced deaths, suicides included, as counts rather than rates; cites the team's own reports that daily heroin use stayed stable from 2001 to 2005, and a police evaluation for the crackdown having ended within weeks of the opening, so that any displacement would, it argues, have lowered deaths near the site before the opening; and reports a fall of 36% among the deaths with signs of injection at the scene (85% of the 89 near the site), with no count, interval or comparison area; it does not reanalyse the study from 2002, answer the fall in reported non-fatal overdoses that the letter cites from the team's earlier work (Kerr et al., 2007), or give the share of deaths without signs of injection in the rest of the city. These three papers describe the background; only the 2006 paper reports overdose deaths, for British Columbia as a whole. In a Vancouver cohort of 1,587 people who inject drugs, enrolled from 1996 to 2004 and interviewed every 6 months (12,030 interviews), the yearly share who reported a non-fatal overdose of any drug in the previous 6 months (12 months, by the letter) was 21% in 1997 and 6% in 2004, with the largest step between about 12% in 2001 and about 5% in 2002, before the site opened, and about 5% to 7% from 2002 to 2004 (read from a figure, approximate; yearly denominators not printed; the figures are not broken down by area); its authors suggest that reduced heroin supply may have played a role and that expanded methadone treatment may also be involved (the letter says they clearly point to supply), had no measure of supply and could not take drug purity into account (Kerr et al., 2007). The study's before period began on 1 January 2001 and so includes that higher year, as does its comparison with the rest of the city. The 2006 paper, by three of the study's authors, compared markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada before and after an Australian heroin shortage that it dates from about January 2001, as yearly averages without tests or a comparison series: overdose deaths in British Columbia (vital statistics, any drug) 297 in 1998–2000 against 192 in 2001–03; ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside 674 against 370 a year (fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03); heroin seized for Canada 184 kg against 67 kg. In its yearly figures (editors' reading, approximate), deaths fell mostly before 2001 (about 399 in 1998, 272 in 1999 and 218 in 2000), were about the same in 2001 (221) and lower in 2002 and 2003 (169 and 186); naloxone use fell in every fiscal year after 1998–99 (about 840 to 350), its last two years inside the study's before period; and seizures were lower in every year from 2001 (about 94, 46 and 60 kg) than in any year before. In the same Vancouver cohort (1,587 participants, May 1996 to December 2004), self-reported daily heroin injection was 36.5% in 1997/98, 32.6% in 1999/00, 23.3% in 2001/02 and 20.8% in 2003/04, by two-year period (adjusted odds ratio 0.55, 0.50 to 0.61, for 2001–04 against 1996–2000). It measured neither purity nor price, has no figures after 2003 (2004 for the cohort) and none for the study's areas, and its authors infer a fall in supply from these markers; it places 2001 in the low period, with deaths that year about level with 2000 and seizures about half of 2000's and twice 2002's. The study cites it for daily heroin injecting of 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting of 17% and 15% and stable methadone use, none of which is in it; the reply cites a different 2006 paper by the same authors and a 2009 web report for that point, neither on file (Wood et al., 2006). The police crackdown in the Downtown Eastside began on 7 April 2003, inside the before period; in its first three months, discarded syringes fell within a block of Main and Hastings (monthly averages 1,082 to 585) and rose in the rest of the Downtown Eastside (784 to 1,253), the only area counted (the letter places the rise in other areas of Vancouver), more cohort members living there said police had changed where they used drugs, and reported daily heroin use and heroin prices did not differ detectably; the paper does not say how long the crackdown lasted (Wood et al., 2004). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an unadjusted before-and-after comparison with changes at the same time) and one for imprecision (few deaths, an interval reaching no fall, a borderline difference between the areas in absolute falls only, and a fall near the site that loses significance when the population is held constant): very low. Rated as worded: an association between the opening of one site and a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 m than elsewhere in Vancouver in 2001–2005; not that supervised injection sites reduce deaths, nor that people who used the site were less likely to die, which the study did not measure. The authors' discussion calls such facilities safe and effective; 'safe' rests on other studies they cite, not on these data, and their conclusion asks that sites be considered for assessment. The drugs: opioids contributed to about half of the deaths and cocaine to about 6 in 10 (editors' sums; a death can involve both), and people at the site injected mostly heroin and powder cocaine; the paper does not mention fentanyl, so it says nothing about a supply in which fentanyl is common. Status single study. Now read against the published letter (Christian et al., 2012) and the authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012), from their PDFs (METHODS §2.3): rating and status unchanged. The letter disputes the cause of the fall, which the claim does not assert, and names two further changes at the same time (a police operation around the site in 2003 and a fall in heroin supply around 2001), now in the statement; it is entered as argument, attributed, since its own data are counts for areas larger than the study's, its police figures rest on an unnamed personal communication and its other figures are second-hand. The study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the 2001 start, and in the letter's own figure the drop from 2001 to 2002 is large in the Vancouver series (about 89 to 49 deaths) and small in the Downtown Eastside series (about 31 to 27; editors' reading). The reply answers the points on area, kinds of death and rates, and adds one restricted reanalysis of the same records (36%, no interval or comparison area), which is not independent replication; its answers on heroin and policing rest on its authors' own reports and a police evaluation, not read here; it leaves the 2001 start, the non-fatal overdose trend and the share of deaths without signs of injection elsewhere unanswered; and its call for such facilities to be central to responses goes beyond the paper's own call for assessment. Which deaths the letter's Downtown Eastside series counts cannot be settled from the two letters (a coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths, by the letter; vital statistics including suicides, by the reply). Also read against the two papers the letter cites that are on file (Kerr et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2004), from their PDFs: rating and status unchanged. Neither measured heroin availability or purity or overdose deaths, and neither reports figures for the study's two areas (within 500 m of the site and the rest of the city), so neither tests the letter's explanations or the study's association. The cohort's fall in self-reported non-fatal overdoses, largest between 2001 and 2002, is a fact about the background in the study's before period, which began in 2001: it fits the letter's point that 2001 was a high year in that cohort, but the study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the same start, the cohort is not split by area, and its authors' reasons (heroin supply, methadone) are suggestions without data on supply. The crackdown began inside the before period, and in its first three months more people living in the Downtown Eastside reported changing where they used drugs and discarded syringes shifted from its core to the rest of the neighbourhood; whether added police stayed after the opening (the letter) or left within weeks of it (the reply), neither paper shows. The letter departs from both papers in places: the cohort's question covered 6 months, not 12; its authors offer reduced supply only as a possible reason, alongside methadone; and the syringe counts that rose were in the rest of the Downtown Eastside, the only area counted, not in other areas of Vancouver (the paper's own abstract speaks of displacement into adjacent areas of the city). Not contested (§6.4): the letter offers no reanalysis of the study's areas and does not change the reading of the claim as worded, an unadjusted association near one site. Also read against the letter's other source on heroin, which the study itself cites too (Wood et al., 2006, dated 2004 in the letter), from its PDF: rating and status unchanged. It is a comparison of periods by three of the study's authors (card sc_wood_2006, ROBINS-E high): it measured no heroin purity, price or availability directly, has no figures after 2003 (2004 for its cohort) and none for the study's two areas, so it tests neither the letter's explanation nor the study's association. Its yearly figures fill in the background. Across British Columbia, overdose deaths fell mostly from 1998 to 2000, were about level in 2001 and lower in 2002 and 2003, which partly fits the letter's point that 2001 had more deaths than later years, but places most of the fall before the study began; the paper itself counts 2001 in the period of reduced supply, and in its figures 2001 was about level with 2000 for deaths and about half of 2000 for seizures, so it shows 2001 neither as clearly high nor as clearly low. Ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside fell in every fiscal year to 2002–03, a fall under way in the site's neighbourhood during the before period that the study's unadjusted two-period comparison cannot separate from the opening, although whether the rest of the city fell alike is not shown. Self-reported daily heroin injection in the team's cohort was lower in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000. The paper does not contain the figures the study cites it for (daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting 17% and 15%, stable methadone use), which leaves the study's statement that drug use stayed constant without a source that can be checked here; the reply's sources for the same point are other reports, not on file. These points add to the reasons for the existing risk-of-bias downgrade rather than changing it, and the rating is already very low. Later evaluations of the same site, on the project's PDF request list, are not on file; the claim must still be read against them before it leaves draft (METHODS §2.3).
