lines.statement: In emergency responders such as police officers and paramedics, evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how often, incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues on the skin causes opioid toxicity (an overdose): no source on file measured responders' exposure or blood levels or counted poisonings among exposed responders, and none of the four, a position statement and three descriptive studies, documents a confirmed case. A 2017 position statement of two North American clinical-toxicology societies, the American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology (AACT) (Moss et al., 2017: eight authors from poison centres, universities, hospitals and a public health institute in the USA and Canada; the recommendations rest on the opinion and clinical experience of a task force of ACMT members and a literature search by the authors; reviewed by an ACMT committee, its board and its members and approved by both societies' boards; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; filed here as a narrative review, so its figures are second-hand and no search method is given), measured no exposure, blood level or responder, and says that its recommendations mainly represent the consensus opinion of experts because data are limited. The two societies judged the risk of clinically significant exposure for responders to be extremely low, and incidental absorption through the skin unlikely (in the recommendations, very unlikely) to cause opioid toxicity. They wrote that they had not seen reports of responders developing signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact, and that the reports they cite (a 2016 warning of the US Drug Enforcement Administration, with two 2017 news reports cited for responders' concern) described nonspecific symptoms, such as dizziness or a feeling that the body was shutting down, without objective signs such as slowed breathing; the incidents are not examined one by one and no count of exposures is given, so the statement could not have detected how often poisoning happens. Their reasoning is arithmetic for fentanyl, not measurement: with both palms covered by fentanyl skin patches, which are made to deliver the drug, about 14 minutes would be needed to absorb 100 micrograms, an amount the statement treats as a high dose without saying why it was chosen (editors' check: 425 micrograms an hour at the stated steady-state rate); they argue that powder or tablets on the skin are taken up more slowly than from a patch and can be brushed or washed off, so that toxicity, if it occurred, would not develop rapidly. At the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, an unprotected person would need nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed), and the statement says that fentanyl's very low vapour pressure suggests evaporation from standing powder is not a practical concern. Splashes to the eyes or mouth are treated as a real route (absorption across mucous membranes more than 30 times that across skin, as stated; one case report of a veterinarian who became drowsy after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, where the authors say the part played by carfentanil is unclear). No estimate is given for carfentanil, described as 10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals, or for any other analogue, although the conclusions cover them; the statement says that the analogues' physical properties suggest a potential for skin absorption and that pharmacological data on other analogues are limited. It concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. It holds that toxicity cannot occur from simply being near the drug, and it still recommends nitrile gloves for routine handling, washing skin with water rather than with alcohol-based sanitizers, and, in the unusual case of significant airborne powder, a properly fitted N95 respirator or P100 mask, which it judges likely to give reasonable protection (its summary says an N95 gives sufficient protection in exceptional circumstances with drug particles or droplets in the air); it adds that individual practitioners may differ. The first data, all descriptive, also find no confirmed case, and none could have found how often one occurs. A review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020: eight authors from an emergency medicine department at Johns Hopkins University, published as an editorial in the journal that carried the position statement, with the statement's last author as its senior author; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared) searched LexisNexis for English-language print and online news from North America published from January 2012 to March 2018: of 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 were on the topic and 214 described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid, and none of the 214 described a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together. Only one incident, in 2016, mentioned any laboratory test of an exposed responder, a urine result reported as traces of opiates, which the authors explain probably came from an opiate screen, a test that does not detect fentanyl or its analogues and, in urine, reflects exposure over the previous several days rather than at the time. The unit is the article, not the incident (distinct incidents are not counted), each article was read by one of five reviewers against criteria the paper does not define, and only the three-part combination is reported, so the zero shows that the news did not report confirmation, mainly because testing was almost never mentioned, not what happened to the responders. A Health Hazard Evaluation by the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH; Jackson et al., 2018) reconstructed one incident in early 2018 from records and from interviews four months later: during a vehicle search, white powder from a locked box blew into the faces of two officers, who within minutes reported difficulty breathing, dizziness and confusion, and a colleague gave one of them naloxone for what was described as shallow breathing and fading consciousness; emergency medical services then found both alert and oriented with normal oxygen saturation, and in the emergency department both had normal-sized pupils and normal heart and breathing rates, neither had any laboratory test, and both went home after more than an hour without symptoms. A field test of the seized substances was reported positive for fentanyl, but the state forensic laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC and no fentanyl or other opioid. Nothing was measured on the officers or in the air, the powder reached their faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and their perceived risk was not assessed; the clinicians who examined them saw no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity, and NIOSH considers it possible that the non-specific symptoms reflected milder toxicity from some drug. In the same report NIOSH states, as its own position and citing the position statement among its sources, that a brief touch of fentanyl powder, or of an analogue, is not expected to be toxic when visible powder is quickly removed. A later NIOSH article (Chiu et al., 2019: seven NIOSH authors, two of whom also wrote that report; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; read as its author manuscript) summarizes two other incidents that NIOSH investigated, from 2017 and 2018, chosen to illustrate different scenarios; neither is the incident of that report. In the first, during a traffic stop, wind blew powder from a container onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, who cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer; within 5 minutes the officer felt disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision, and ambulance staff washed the skin with water and found the officer alert, with pupils of 4 mm, a breathing rate of 17 a minute and raised blood pressure and heart rate; no laboratory test was done, the officer was discharged with an assessment of chemical exposure, and the laboratory later found fentanyl with methamphetamine in the powder left in the container. In the second, four officers became lightheaded or dizzy, among other symptoms, after a call to a hotel room with drug powders in view: three who had entered the room, about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began, and one who never entered, 30 to 45 minutes after handling a camera and other items from the room that showed no visible contamination; one officer slumped to the ground and improved rapidly after a colleague gave naloxone; none was reported to have depressed breathing (one officer's breathing rate ranged from 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department), all were alert with no documented constricted pupils, and their urine screens, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative; the laboratory found fentanyl, a fentanyl analogue, heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones in the room. Nothing was measured in the air, on surfaces or skin, or in blood, and perceived risk was not assessed. The authors judge that no officer's effects were consistent with severe opioid toxicity, consider breathing in, the lining of the eyes, nose or mouth, swallowing and the skin all possible routes, and read the one officer's improvement after naloxone as suggesting that opioids played a substantial part, an inference from one uncontrolled observation in an officer whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; like NIOSH's report, they state that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic when visible contamination is promptly removed, and they add that alcohol-based hand sanitizer may increase absorption. None of these studies can show that no responder has ever been poisoned: news reports are a selected record in which testing was almost never mentioned, and three incidents, investigated because officers fell ill, give no rate. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (for the absence of a confirmed case only).
lines.population: Emergency responders (law enforcement and emergency medical services) in North America who may meet fentanyl or fentanyl analogues as powder, tablets or liquid on calls, at crime scenes or in drug raids: as considered in a 2017 position statement, which studied no responders, exposures or cases; as reported in 214 English-language North American news articles (January 2012 to March 2018) that described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid; and two sheriff's department officers in one incident in early 2018, investigated afterwards by NIOSH, and five police officers in two other incidents of 2017 and 2018, also investigated afterwards by NIOSH (Chiu et al., 2019)
lines.exposure: Incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues: on the skin (the question here), and also airborne powder breathed in, splashes to the eyes or mouth, and being near the drug; reasoned from pharmacokinetic data in the position statement, as reported in news articles (routes recorded but not reported), and, in the NIOSH incident, white powder of unknown composition blown into two officers' faces; in the two incidents of Chiu et al., powder blown onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, which the laboratory later found to contain fentanyl with methamphetamine, and a hotel room with drug powders in view, with items from it handled elsewhere; no source measured any exposure
lines.comparator: None in any source: the position statement collected no data, and its worked arithmetic takes as its reference the time needed to absorb 100 micrograms of fentanyl through the skin, or the exposure needed to reach a dose of 100 micrograms from the air, an amount it does not justify; the news review and the incident investigations had no comparison group
lines.outcome: Clinically significant opioid toxicity in the responder (objective signs such as slowed breathing or a lowered level of consciousness), as distinct from nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness or anxiety; in the news review, a confirmed exposure (an article describing a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together); in the NIOSH incidents, symptoms and clinical findings in emergency medical service and emergency department records (with urine drug screens, unable to detect fentanyl, in four officers), and forensic analysis of the substances seized
lines.magnitude: No measured rate or count of poisonings. ACMT and AACT position (Moss et al., 2017): risk of clinically significant exposure extremely low; no reports seen of responders with signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact; incidental skin absorption unlikely (summary) or very unlikely (recommendations) to cause toxicity. Worked arithmetic, fentanyl only: both palms covered by fentanyl patches (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%, delivery 2.5 micrograms per cm2 per hour at steady state), about 14 minutes to absorb 100 micrograms (editors' check: 170 cm2 × 2.5 = 425 micrograms an hour, so 14.1 minutes); patches take 3–13 hours to give a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 hours to peak; at the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed); vapour pressure 4.6 × 10^-6 Pa. Mucous membranes: more than 30-fold the absorption of skin; one case report of drowsiness after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, its cause unclear to the authors. No estimate for carfentanil (10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals) or any other analogue. Respiratory protection: an N95 respirator or P100 mask likely to give reasonable protection against significant airborne powder (recommendations); an N95 sufficient in exceptional circumstances with particles or droplets in the air (summary). Herman et al. (2020), English-language North American print and online news (LexisNexis), January 2012 to March 2018: 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 relevant (editors: 72%), 214 describing a specific responder exposure (editors: 21% of relevant); 0 of 214 with a plausible route, consistent symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing together; any laboratory testing of an exposed person mentioned for 1 incident (2 articles; editors: 0.9% of 214), an opiate urine result; distinct incidents not counted, and no count reported for any single criterion. Jackson et al. (2018; NIOSH), 1 incident, 2 officers: no laboratory test of either officer; no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity in EMS or emergency department records (alert and oriented, normal oxygen saturation, normal-sized pupils, normal heart and respiratory rates in the emergency department, blood pressure raised); observed for more than an hour and discharged; naloxone given to one officer at the scene; seized items: cocaine, methamphetamine and THC identified, alprazolam and sodium bicarbonate only indicated, no fentanyl or other opioid, against a presumptive field result for fentanyl; no exposure measured. Chiu et al. (2019; NIOSH), 2 incidents, 5 officers: no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl (HHE 1, no laboratory test; HHE 2, urine screens negative for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates, with cut-offs of 500 ng/mL for amphetamines and 150 ng/mL for cocaine; opiate screens do not detect fentanyl); HHE 1: onset within 5 minutes; first vital signs blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17, heart rate 105, pupils 4 mm and reactive; later heart rate 80–85, breathing rate 15–21, blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104; powder left in the container 1.56 g, fentanyl and methamphetamine identified; HHE 2: onset about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began for the three officers who entered the room and about 30 to 45 minutes after handling items for the fourth; one dose of intranasal naloxone to one officer, with rapid improvement; no depressed breathing reported; one breathing rate of 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department; hotel-room evidence: fentanyl 0.14 g, heroin 0.14 g, N-ethylpentylone 2.87 g, para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl, dibutylone, and cocaine and methamphetamine residues; no exposure measured; perceived risk not assessed.
lines.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November with the first data on file, a review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020) and a NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation (Jackson et al., 2018), both read from their PDFs. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review, but its certainty stays very low and its relation insufficient evidence. All four sources are observational, so the start is low (METHODS §6.3): the news review is a case series of media-reported incidents, the evaluation a single case report, Chiu et al. a case series of two further incidents, and the position statement, filed as a narrative review, starts from the design of what it describes (pharmacokinetic studies of fentanyl patches and of inhaled fentanyl, a patch product label, industrial exposure limits, one small volunteer study, one case report, one animal study and agency warnings, none randomized and none a study of exposed responders). Down one level for risk of bias: the statement's unsystematic selection and consensus opinion, the news review's undefined criteria applied by one reviewer per article with incidents not counted, and the evaluation's reconstruction from records and interviews four months later with nothing measured; all four share one gap, the absence of any measurement of exposure, so one level, not two. Down one for indirectness: patch and industrial data applied to powder on the skin (fentanyl only), news text instead of medical, police or laboratory records, and one incident in which the powder reached the officers' faces and no opioid was found in the seized items: very low, the floor, so imprecision (no source can give a rate) is not counted again. Inconsistency is now assessable and absent: none of the four reports a confirmed case. The new data do not raise the rating because both are descriptive records with no denominator of exposures: the news review's zero follows mainly from testing almost never being mentioned (one incident, two articles), so it shows that the news did not report confirmation, not that no responder was poisoned; and the evaluation tested neither officer, so it can neither confirm nor exclude poisoning in that incident, while its laboratory found no opioid in what was seized. Companion paper of 13 November: Chiu et al. (2019), NIOSH's account of two further incidents with five officers, read as its author manuscript, adds no confirmed case and no measurement, and does not change the rating: the officer onto whom powder later found to contain fentanyl with methamphetamine was blown had non-specific symptoms within 5 minutes, no recorded sign of opioid toxicity and no laboratory test; in the other incident the urine screens, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative, and the authors' reading of one officer's rapid improvement after naloxone as a sign of opioid involvement rests on one uncontrolled observation. Its incidents are not the one in the NIOSH report (other evaluation numbers, other details), but two of its authors wrote that report. The relation stays insufficient evidence: no source measured exposure, so neither poisoning from skin contact nor its absence can be shown with any precision, and none could have detected how often poisoning happens. The societies' judgment that the risk is extremely low and that skin absorption is unlikely, or very unlikely, to cause toxicity is reported as their judgment, with their own hedges (unlikely, very unlikely, likely to give reasonable protection), and NIOSH's statement on brief skin contact as NIOSH's own position, which cites the societies' statement among its sources; neither is adopted as the editors' finding. Where the statement's summary is firmer than the section it summarizes (an N95 gives sufficient protection, against an N95 or P100 likely to give reasonable protection), both are given. The single quotation records the statement's own description of its basis. Not used: the statement's naloxone section and NIOSH's recommendations, in the 2018 report and in Chiu et al. (guidance, which this answer does not cover), the second-hand figures on deaths from synthetic opioids, and the news review's untested suggestions (a nocebo effect; protective equipment delaying care). Status replicated, for the absence of a confirmed case only (METHODS §6.4): two independent primary studies of different design, the news review (by a Johns Hopkins team whose senior author is the position statement's last author) and the NIOSH evaluation, agree that no confirmed opioid poisoning was documented, as the statement says from its authors' knowledge; none measured exposure, and none can show that no responder was ever poisoned. Chiu et al. agree, but they share two authors with the NIOSH evaluation and are not counted as a third independent study. The four anchors from Chiu et al. (16 to 19) are ai-located and await a second reader's check.

lines.q: Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?
lines.short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.
lines.but: Nobody has measured real touches, and finding no proven case is not proof it never happens.
how: Poison experts worked out that palms covered in fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver it, would need about 14 minutes to pass a high dose.
Researchers checked 214 news stories about police or paramedics exposed to opioids. Only one incident mentioned any test, probably one that misses fentanyl.
A federal safety agency looked into three cases where seven officers felt ill. It found no signs of a serious overdose. No officer had a test that finds fentanyl.
Splashes into the eyes or mouth are treated as a real risk. No sums were done for carfentanil, far stronger than morphine in animals.

lines.statement: In police officers and other emergency responders in the United States, surveyed at trainings in Missouri in 2019 (Winograd et al., 2020) and Indiana in 2020–2021 (del Pozo et al., 2021) and online in New York State in 2019 (Persaud & Jennings, 2020), and interviewed at five law enforcement agencies in 2020 (Attaway et al., 2021), the belief that touching fentanyl can cause an overdose, or in New York that briefly touching it could be deadly, was held by about 4 in 5 of those surveyed, and concern about it was voiced by nearly all of those interviewed who were asked; answers given just after a training that included a 10-minute module correcting it disagreed with it far more often, but these before-and-after comparisons, with no comparison group or later follow-up and many participants missing, cannot show that the training changed the belief, or for how long. The studies measured what responders believed and said, not what fentanyl does: whether touching fentanyl can cause an overdose is a separate question (see 'Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?': evidence insufficient, no confirmed case on file), and the papers call the belief false or misinformation on the strength of the 2017 position statement of two clinical-toxicology societies and similar sources, not their own data. Before a 2-hour overdose-response training in the Eastern Region of Missouri (11 sessions, January to August 2019, reaching 200 participants, of whom 140 were analysed: 113 law enforcement or security officers and 27 emergency medical or fire department workers), 20.9% answered False to the True/False item "I can overdose from touching fentanyl." (law enforcement 16.8%, 19 of 113; emergency medical 37.0%, 10 of 27; 29 of 140, 20.7%, by the editors' arithmetic), so about 4 in 5 did not. Before a 3-hour harm-reduction and occupational-safety training (SHIELD) held by Zoom for Indiana officers from December 2020 to June 2021 (204 attendees from 49 counties, of whom 129, 63.2%, answered the baseline survey), 103 of 129 (79.8%; Wilson 95% interval about 72% to 86%, editors' calculation) agreed, 52 of them strongly, with a 6-point item saying that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it; 79 of the 129 (61.2%) had earlier had fentanyl exposure precaution training. Neither sample was random: both were attendees of trainings in one Midwestern state each, answering a single unvalidated item. In an online pilot survey of police, fire and emergency medical workers serving New York State (Persaud & Jennings, 2020: February and March 2019; spread through 3 of 15 associations asked, flyers and personal contacts, so no response rate can be known; 187 analysed of 247 responses), 149 of 187 (79.7%; about 73% to 85%, editors' calculation) agreed with a statement that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: 86 of 92 in law enforcement (93.5%) and 63 of 95 in fire, emergency medical services or both (66.3%); the six answer levels are reported only as agree or disagree, so slight and strong agreement cannot be told apart. Asked where they got information on fentanyl exposure and safety (all that apply), most named seminars or courses (78.1%) and department training (76.5%), 67.4% federal agencies and 13.9% news media, but no answer was linked to its source, and the authors' suggestion that overreliance on media reports lies behind the belief rests on no analysis. In interviews at five purposively chosen agencies (January to May 2020; 23 officers and leaders analysed, 20 of them asked open questions about fentanyl), nearly all of those asked said they were concerned that encountering fentanyl might put them at risk of an overdose and a few were not, with no counts given for any theme; they named other officers, law enforcement professional organizations, a Drug Enforcement Administration roll-call training video shown at in-service training (released in 2016 according to Attaway et al.; Herman et al., 2020, give the same video, at the same Justice Department web address, as of 6 June 2017), and regional intelligence bulletins as their sources; over one third of officers had heard of someone in their own agency overdosing, but none could say for certain that the substance was fentanyl or that the colleague had overdosed; two said they had been exposed themselves without symptoms; and a handful who were asked did not know the toxicology societies' statement. The interview study's abstract, saying that nearly all those interviewed wrongly believed skin contact was deadly, is sharper than its Results. In online US news found through Media Cloud for January 2015 to September 2019 (Beletsky et al., 2020), 506 of 551 relevant articles (92%) were coded as misinformation, a category that included any article giving an anecdotal account of an overdose blamed on casual contact, with its rumoured symptoms, so neutral incident reports counted, against 45 corrective or partially corrective articles, 18 of them unequivocally corrective; misinformation articles received 450,011 Facebook shares, against 48,235 for the corrective or partially corrective and 29,652 for the unequivocally corrective (about 15 to 1 against the last group, the abstract's figure, and about 9 to 1 against all 45, editors' calculation); the authors' potential reach of 69,751,705 is shares multiplied by an assumed 155 contacts, an upper bound on views, not a count of people, although the abstract presents it as people reached; and the two most-shared stories, as the authors summarize news reports, concerned two Ohio officers, one whose powder and overdose were never confirmed by laboratory testing and one whose substance was later confirmed as methamphetamine. Counting articles and shares cannot show that the coverage shaped officers' beliefs. Immediately after the Missouri training, which included about 10 minutes on contact with fentanyl, 83.6% answered False (law enforcement 81.4%, emergency medical 92.6%; 117 of 140 by the editors' arithmetic), so about 1 in 6 did not; of the 69 Indiana officers (53.5% of baseline respondents, 34% of attendees) who completed a follow-up linked to their baseline, 27 (39.1%; about 28% to 51%, editors' calculation) still agreed and 42 (60.9%) disagreed, 22 of them strongly, and their mean score moved from 2.2 to 4.0 on the scale from 1 (strongly agree) to 6 (strongly disagree) (paired t = 6.52, p < .001). Neither study had a comparison group or a later follow-up; the second answers came after the trainers had given the answer, from people who knew what was wanted; 43 of the 200 Missouri participants are unaccounted for and no paired counts are reported; two-thirds of the Indiana attendees are missing from its before-and-after comparison, whose abstract sets 79.8% of 129 against 39.1% of 69; and any change belongs to the whole training, not to the 10-minute module alone. The Indiana paper's printed effect sizes are wrong: its Cohen's d of 2.33 for the change is incompatible with its t and n, and by the editors' calculation the standardized change is about d_z = 0.78, the printed 2.33 matching the standard deviation of the paired differences and the printed interval [1.05, 0.51] matching that of d_z rather than that of the 1.8-point mean change (about 1.25 to 2.35). The two training studies share two authors (Goulka, Beletsky), and Beletsky is also first author of the media study; the trainings were developed or are delivered by the authors' teams, and both evaluations were publicly funded (in Missouri through the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, in Indiana through a CDC Overdose Data to Action grant); the New York survey, by two authors at John Jay College of Criminal Justice with no funding beyond administrative support, shares no author with them. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (for the share holding the belief, now found by independent teams; the answers after training come from one team only).
lines.population: Police officers and other emergency responders in the United States: 140 responders analysed (113 law enforcement or security officers and 27 emergency medical or fire department workers; mean age 40.96, 110 men) of 200 people reached by 11 overdose-response trainings in the Eastern Region of Missouri, January to August 2019; 129 of 204 Indiana officers from 49 counties who attended three SHIELD trainings held by Zoom between December 2020 and June 2021 and answered the baseline survey (mean age 45.1, 97 men), 69 of whom also answered the follow-up; 23 officers and agency leaders at five purposively chosen US law enforcement agencies, interviewed from January to May 2020, 20 of them asked about fentanyl; 187 New York State police, fire and emergency medical workers (92 in law enforcement; 95 in fire, emergency medical services or both) who answered an online pilot survey in February and March 2019, of 247 responses; and, for news coverage, 551 online US news articles from January 2015 to September 2019
lines.exposure: For the beliefs and their sources, none: what responders answered or said before any training or in an online survey, and online news articles coded for their message, with their Facebook shares; for the change, attending a training that included about 10 minutes of corrective information on contact with fentanyl (a 2-hour in-person overdose-response training in Missouri; a 3-hour SHIELD harm-reduction and occupational-safety training by Zoom in Indiana, led by a former police officer)
lines.comparator: None outside the trainees: the same people's answers just before the training (in Missouri everyone analysed, with no paired counts reported; in Indiana the 69 linked completers); no untrained comparison group and no later follow-up; in the news study, corrective and partially corrective articles against misinformation articles; in the New York survey, none (law enforcement and fire or emergency medical workers are reported side by side)
lines.outcome: Answers to single belief items (True or False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl, in Missouri; agreement on a 6-point scale with an item that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, in Indiana; agreement on a 6-point scale, reported only as agree or disagree, with a statement that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, in New York); concern about overdose from encountering fentanyl and the sources named, in interviews, and the information sources ticked in the New York survey; for news articles, the authors' coding as misinformation, corrective or partially corrective, Facebook shares and modelled potential views

(2021), five agencies, January to May 2020: 38 interviewed, 23 analysed (12 officers who had given naloxone, 5 who had not, 6 leaders; 18 men, 15 Caucasian), 20 asked the fentanyl questions; themes reported with verbal quantifiers only (nearly all, a few, a handful, over one third, two). Beletsky et al. (2020), January 2015 to September 2019: 551 articles (47 national, 504 state and local; 48 states), 506 misinformation (printed 92%; 37 national), 45 corrective or partially corrective (8%; 8 national), 18 unequivocally corrective; Facebook shares 450,011, 48,235 and 29,652 (editors: ratios 15.2 and 9.3; the printed 6.6% of total is 6.6% of misinformation shares, 6.0% of all 498,246); potential views, shares × 155: 69,751,705 for misinformation and 4,596,060 for the 18 corrective articles, upper bounds; DEA video in 80 articles; most-shared story 133,751 shares, the next 45,533. lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3): it reports how many responders said they held the belief, where they said it came from, how news coverage carried it, and how answers differed just after a training; it does not claim that training changed beliefs, which these designs cannot show. Descriptive, observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias (training attendees and a self-selected online sample rather than random samples, heavy missing data, single unvalidated items, second answers given straight after the corrective message, interviews without counts) and one for indirectness (two Midwestern states, New York State and five agencies in 2019 to 2021; items about overdose, and in New York about death, one combining touching with inhaling; answers rather than behaviour): very low. Not upgraded: descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect, and the before-and-after shifts are not estimates of an effect. Rated as worded: as estimates of a training effect, both training studies are at critical risk of bias under ROBINS-I (no comparison group, an immediate post-test, attrition), so a claim that training changes the belief would also be very low, and the statement says that the designs cannot show it. The single quotation records the Missouri item itself, because its wording is the measure; the Indiana item, 17 words long, is paraphrased. Editors' calculations (Wilson intervals; counts from the printed group percentages; the recomputed standardized effects, d about 0.40 and 0.56 and d_z about 0.78; the interval for the paired change; the ratios of shares) are labelled for the second reader to recompute. Printed figures corrected or qualified: the Missouri overall 20.9% fits 29 of 139, not of 140 (20.7%), and its differences are percentage points; the Indiana Cohen's d values (2.33, 1.61, 2.33) are incompatible with the printed t and group sizes, its paired interval matches d_z rather than the mean change, and its printed patrol means contradict the stated direction; the Indiana abstract's 79.8% against 39.1% mixes denominators of 129 and 69 and calls a 3-hour training with a 10-minute module a 10-minute online training; the news study's 6.6% of total is 6.6% of misinformation shares (6.0% of all), and its 70 million people reached are an upper bound on views; and the interview study's abstract says more than its Results. Beliefs are reported as beliefs: the papers' description of the belief as false rests on the 2017 ACMT and AACT position statement and similar sources, and this project rates that question separately (very low certainty, insufficient evidence, no confirmed case on file), so the answer says what people believed, not whether they were right. Status replicated (METHODS §6.4), for the share holding the belief: the New York survey (Persaud & Jennings, 2020), which shares no author with the others, finds about 4 in 5 agreeing that a brief touch could be deadly, as the two training surveys find for overdose; those two share two authors (Goulka, Beletsky), and Beletsky is also first author of the news study; the interview study shares no author with them (one of its authors and Beletsky list the same University of California, San Diego division) and agrees that concern was near universal among those asked, but without counts it cannot replicate the figures. The answers just after training come from one team only (replicated by the same team, METHODS §6.3), as the statement says. Companion paper of 13 November: the New York survey, cited second-hand through Attaway et al. (nearly 80%) in the earlier version, is now read first-hand (Persaud & Jennings, 2020): its 79.7% is agreement, at levels it does not report, in a self-selected sample; it adds a third state, a statement about death rather than overdose, and the only counts of information sources on file, which it did not link to the belief. Not used: its items on gloves, hand sanitizer and protective equipment (practice rather than the belief about touching), its claim, cited to the 2017 position statement, that harm from touching fentanyl is chronic for people who touch it regularly (which the statement does not say), and the papers' views on stress, stigma, wasted resources and delayed overdose response, which they did not measure. The DEA roll-call video is dated by each paper's own account: 2016 in Attaway et al., 6 June 2017 in Herman et al. (anchor 15), at the same web address. The four anchors added on 13 November (12 to 15) and the reworded anchor 8 await a second reader's check, and card sc_persaud_2020 its round-2 reading.

lines.q: Do police believe touching fentanyl can cause overdose? Does training change that?
lines.short: In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death. Right after trainings, far fewer did.
lines.but: No survey picked people at random. Answers came right after training, with no untrained group or later check.
how: In Missouri, only about 1 in 5 of 140 police, paramedics and firefighters rejected the idea before training; about 5 in 6 did right after.
Officers in five US police forces said they heard it from colleagues, a federal drug agency video and bulletins; none could confirm a colleague's overdose.
506 of 551 US news articles were coded misinformation, even plain reports of ill officers. They got about 450,000 Facebook shares; clear corrections, under 30,000.
In a 2019 New York online survey, 149 of 187 police, fire and ambulance workers agreed a brief touch could be deadly. Most named courses and training as sources; about 1 in 7, the news.

lines.statement: In people studied from 1967 to 1970, both people given pharmaceutical LSD in medical or research settings and people who reported taking LSD outside them, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD, compared with no LSD or with each person's own sample from before LSD, changes chromosome breakage. Six of the primary studies have been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), among them the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage after LSD; the others, including the later and larger studies of those two laboratories and the study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968), are known only through one 1971 narrative review in Science (Dishotsky et al., 1971; figures second-hand; no search method or selection criteria stated; supported in part by the State of California Department of Mental Hygiene and by Mendocino State Hospital, where two of the authors worked; its tables include the authors' own unpublished study, and its second author, W. D. Loughman, was the first author of one of the negative studies, Loughman et al., 1967). What these studies measured was breaks seen under a microscope in chromosomes of white blood cells taken from the blood and made to divide in a culture dish, counted as breaks per cell in some studies and as the share of cells with any aberration in others, in groups of 1 to 46 people, by laboratories whose breakage rates in unexposed controls ranged from 0% to 11.9%; most breaks recorded were of a kind that the review's authors say mostly arises from the culture procedure itself, and they limit their own conclusion to damage detectable by the methods then available. The concern began with Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), as Tjio et al. (1969) note, mainly a study of cells in a dish, not of people: LSD added to cultured white blood cells from two donors, whose results were pooled, was followed by 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 conditions of concentration and exposure time, against 0.037 (34 breaks in 925 cells) in untreated cultures from six people, with no statistical test of the difference (the review nonetheless lists it as significant) and, in the paper's own Table 1, no steady rise with concentration; its one patient, a man given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy who had also been treated with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, had 12% breakage in 200 cells 8 months after his last session, against the 3.7% of untreated cultures from other people, with no sample from before LSD (the same laboratory's later report lists, as its case 37, a man of 52 who had taken LSD 15 times, the last 8 months before sampling, with phenothiazines as his only other drug and 39 breaks in 300 cells; he matches this patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, but neither paper says whether he is the same man). Later in 1967 the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage, both read in full, compared people who had taken LSD with people who had not, with coded slides but no samples from before LSD and no statistical comparison of the groups in either paper. Irwin and Egozcue (1967) found on average 23.6 breaks per 100 cells in 8 men who reported taking LSD an estimated 4 to 200 times (its source not stated; some had also taken cannabis, mescaline or peyote, psilocybin or DMT, not counted) against 11.9 in 9 volunteers who had not taken it (editors' calculation; 95% interval of the difference about 3.7 to 19.7), with overlapping ranges, no women in the LSD group, and the two highest control rates in people with x-ray exposure. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) found 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD, every one of whom had also taken other drugs or medicines (amphetamines 15, phenothiazines 10) and whose recruitment and source of LSD are not described, against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 controls without drugs, after two controls with 31.0 and 14.0 were left out for a viral illness that began within a day of sampling (5.4 breaks per 100 cells with them, pooled; 6.5 as the mean of the 14 controls' rates); yet 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (three of them chlorpromazine, two of them boys aged 9) had similar rates, 12.6 on average, no different from the LSD patients (editors' calculation; the paper makes no such comparison); and 4 children exposed to LSD before birth had 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults. Two other small cross-sectional studies found no excess: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people who reported heavy recent use of illicit LSD (7 of them also amphetamines), scored by someone who did not know their drug histories, against none in 112 cells from one concurrent control and 1 in 561 cells from 18 earlier controls of the same laboratory (Loughman et al., 1967); and 2.2 breaks per 100 cells (21 in 937) in 4 psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and 1.5 (14 in 914) in 4 patients given LSD in treatment, against 1.6 (15 in 950) in 4 hospital volunteers, with each sample cultured in two laboratories and blinding of the scorers not reported (Sparkes et al., 1968); groups this small cannot exclude a modest rise. The strongest study, Tjio et al. (1969), sampled 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis before and 1 to 10 days after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with coded samples scored by one reader who did not know whether a sample came before or after LSD: the share of cells with chromosome aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not a significant change (P = 0.3; 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 percentage points, editors' calculation); 3 patients had large rises (to 23.08%, 43.92% and 14.16%), and the 2 of them who could be retested were back within the normal range 71 and 229 days later (one still 2.32 points above his own earlier rate); there was no untreated comparison group, and 31 of the 32 had been given other medicines in hospital before their first sample. Cohen, Marinello, et al. and Tjio et al. both used LSD supplied by Sandoz Pharmaceuticals. What these designs can show is limited: cells in a dish are not people, blood cells are not sperm or egg cells (none of these studies examined those), and pharmaceutical LSD given in hospital is not street LSD of unknown content. In the review's tallies, of 310 people in 21 reports from 17 laboratories, at most 18 of 126 given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%) had breakage above their control group's average (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient is counted among the first; if he is also Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s case 37, he is counted among the second as well). The early reports of raised breakage in people, from 1967 on, came from three teams studying people who used many illicit drugs (80 of 86 people studied by two of them had raised rates; the first report of each is read, as above, the later ones are not), whereas nine other teams studying similar people (88 people, editors' sum from Table 2, including those of Loughman et al. and Sparkes et al.) found none beyond that in the general population apart from one infant exposed before birth; nearly all of these people used other drugs too (of 77 with raised rates and detailed drug histories, 43 had used amphetamine), Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had rates similar to their LSD patients (above), whom the review counts as exposed to illicit LSD although the paper does not say where their LSD came from, and only 54% of 57 street samples sold as LSD contained it in relatively pure form. Among people given pharmaceutical LSD, the review's comparisons with unexposed controls found raised breakage in at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), all but one (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient) reported by one team whose methods the review's authors criticize (as few as 3 of 61, 4.9%, leaving out that team's incomplete data); in 56 people tested before and after, 6 (10.7%) had raised breakage afterwards, 3 of them after LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968, as the review describes it) and 1 with a viral infection, and the review says the 5 of these 6 who were retested 2 weeks to 7.67 months later were back at their earlier rates (in Tjio et al.'s own figures, one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate); only the intravenous study (3 people) showed a significant group change (1.0% to 4.78%), and in Tjio et al.'s study, which the review counts as 37 patients, the 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before, reported with the 32 patients, went from 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from the paper's own Table 4, editors' calculation), not significantly. In cells exposed to LSD in a dish, 6 of 9 studies found more breaks, mostly at concentrations or exposure times the review's authors judge unreachable in people, and in one study aspirin raised breakage about as much as LSD (9.6% and 10.2% of cells, against 5.0% in untreated cells); in Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s cultures, 7.7 to 17.5 breaks per 100 cells against 3.9, with no statistical test and no rise across a 10,000-fold range of concentrations. On cancer, the review found no significant research, only three case reports of leukaemia or other cancers in about four years, and it says that, as of then, there appeared to be no definite evidence that LSD causes cancer. On birth defects, no malformation had been reported after pharmaceutical LSD and six after illicit LSD (several of the mothers also used other drugs), which the review's authors say may be coincidence; of 14 children exposed to illicit LSD before birth, 10 had raised breakage and all were healthy without birth defects (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s 4 children, 2 of them with high rates against adult controls and none with obvious abnormalities, belong to a report the review does not cite for this count); and in a series of 148 pregnancies, spontaneous abortions occurred in 37% when parents had used both pharmaceutical and illicit LSD, against 15% with pharmaceutical LSD alone and 20% in the general population, but only 12 of the pregnancies involved LSD during gestation and one woman accounted for 5 of the 10 abortions in the combined group. Animal results were inconsistent: in fruit flies, mutations appeared only at concentrations the review's authors call extremely high; malformations were seen in some mouse strains but not others; and of four pregnant rhesus monkeys given repeated injections at 100 or more times the usual human experimental dose, two delivered stillborn infants with facial deformities and one infant died at a month, which the review calls preliminary but suggestive. In the editors' reading, the review authors' closing statement that they believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man goes beyond this evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
lines.population: People whose blood cells were examined from 1967 to 1970. Read in full: cultured white blood cells from two donors and one man treated with LSD in psychotherapy (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967); 8 men reporting LSD use against 9 volunteers without it (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967); 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD, 12 drug-free controls (2 more left out), 4 children exposed before birth and cultured cells from 6 donors (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use against 19 laboratory controls (Loughman et al., 1967); three groups of 4, namely hospital volunteers, psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and patients given LSD in treatment (Sparkes et al., 1968); and 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before (Tjio et al., 1969). As summarized in one narrative review: 21 reports from 17 laboratories with 310 people, 126 given pharmaceutical (pure) LSD in medical or research settings (many of them patients, some treated with psychiatric medicines) and 184 who had used illicit drugs sold as LSD (nearly all of whom also used other drugs), in groups of 1 to 46 people, 56 of the 126 tested before and after LSD; children exposed before birth reported separately (14 exposed to illicit LSD); also cultured cells, fruit flies, a fungus, rodents and monkeys
lines.exposure: Pharmaceutical LSD given under supervision (one to three treatments in the before-and-after studies, by mouth except in one study of 3 people given it into a vein; more in some comparison studies, for example 15 sessions in Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient), or self-reported use of LSD outside medical settings, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, of unknown content and strength (the source is not stated in Irwin & Egozcue, 1967, or Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); in laboratory studies, LSD added to cultured cells
lines.comparator: Unexposed control groups (breakage rates of 0% to 11.9% between laboratories), each person's own sample from before LSD (with no untreated group sampled at the same times in the largest study), untreated cultures in the cell studies, or, in one study, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967)
lines.outcome: Chromosome breakage, mostly chromatid-type breaks, counted under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture (as breaks per cell or as the share of cells with an aberration, which differ between studies); also, as reported in the review, case reports of cancer, birth defects and spontaneous abortions after LSD, mutations in fruit flies and a fungus, and malformations in rodents and monkeys
lines.magnitude: Primary studies read in full. Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors: 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 LSD conditions against 0.037 (34 of 925 cells) in untreated cultures, no statistical test (384 breaks in 2678 treated cells, 0.143 per cell, editors' sum); one patient 12% in 200 cells, no sample from before LSD. Irwin & Egozcue (1967): breaks per 100 cells 12.0 to 38.0 in 8 men reporting LSD use against 7.0 to 25.0 in 9 volunteers without it; means 23.6 against 11.9 (378 of 1600 and 215 of 1800 cells; difference 11.7, 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7, editors' calculation; the review prints 23.4% against 11.0% in its text and 11.9% in its table); P < .05 for 6 of 8 and 1 of 9 people, test not named. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967): 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 drug-free controls, no test (difference 9.3, 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3, editors' calculation; with the 2 controls left out after a viral illness included, 5.4 pooled (161 in 2974) and a per-person mean of 6.5, a difference in per-person means of 6.6, 1.5 to 11.7); 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD 12.6 (mean of six rates; 161 in 1361 cells), not different from the LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84, editors' calculation); 4 children exposed before birth 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults; cells in a dish from 6 donors 7.7 to 17.5 against 3.9 (1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells, editors' sum; the review lists 8725 cells), no concentration-response, no test. Loughman et al. (1967): 0 chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people (95% limits 0.0% to 0.5%) against 0 of 112 (1 concurrent control), 1 of 561 (0.2%; 18 earlier controls) and 11 of 1569 (0.7%; published controls), not significant. Sparkes et al. (1968): breaks per 100 cells 2.2 (21/937; LSD taken privately, 4 people), 1.5 (14/914; LSD in treatment, 4) and 1.6 (15/950; controls, 4); cells with a break 1.4%, 1.4% and 1.5%; not significant (with 4 against 4 the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.029, editors' calculation). Tjio et al. (1969), 32 patients before and after one dose: cells with aberrations 4.28% to 5.91% (+1.63 points; P = 0.3; lower dose level, 11 patients, 4.05% to 9.26%, P = 0.15; higher, 21 patients, 4.39% to 4.16%, P = 0.8); editors' calculation: 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 points, 18 rose, 12 fell, 2 unchanged; 3 rises of more than 4 points (2.44% to 23.08%, 9.50% to 43.92%, 1.48% to 14.16%), 2 retested at 4.76% (71 days) and 1.48% (229 days); 5 volunteers with earlier illicit use 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from Table 4, editors' calculation), not significant. Dishotsky et al. (1971), counts without intervals: breakage above control means in at most 18 of 126 people given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%; 45.98%, 80 of 174, without one study's incomplete data); 18 of the 108 people reported with damage had pharmaceutical LSD (16.67%). Illicit-LSD studies: 80 of 86 raised in two early teams' studies (for example 18.76% against 9.03% in 46 people, and 13.2% against 3.8% in 18); none beyond the general population in nine other teams' studies (88 people, editors' sum). Pharmaceutical LSD compared with unexposed controls: at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), as few as 3 of 61 (4.9%). Before and after: 6 of 56 raised (10.7%); group averages 5.7% to 4.9% (10 people), 0.0% to 0.0% (6), 2.81% to 3.57% (5) and 4.28% to 5.91% (32), not significant; 1.0% to 4.78% after intravenous LSD (3 people), significant; 50 of 53 given LSD by mouth (94.3%) showed no increase. Other drugs: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD 12.6% against 13.2% in 18 patients with LSD and other drugs, not significantly different by the review's own comparison (the paper reports none; editors' check above). In vitro: 6 of 9 studies positive; in one study LSD 10.2%, aspirin 9.6% and ergonovine 10.0% against 5.0% in control cells. Pregnancies: spontaneous abortion 37% (pharmaceutical plus illicit LSD), 15% (pharmaceutical only), 20% (general population), in 148 pregnancies with 12 exposed during gestation.
lines.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November because four of the primary studies had been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3); later that day the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage were read in full too (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), without a change of rating. The human primary studies are observational, four cross-sectional comparisons and one before-and-after study without an untreated group, and start low; the cell-culture studies are preclinical and can only be indirect for people (§5.4). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision (domain notes): very low, the floor; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down twice, with the same result. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither an increase in breakage after LSD nor its absence can be shown with precision (§6.1): in the strongest study the share of cells with aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not significantly, with a 95% interval of the change (about −1.3 to +4.6 points, editors' calculation) that includes no change and a rise to about double, and 3 of 32 patients had large rises, back within the normal range in the 2 retested; the two cross-sectional studies that found no excess (8 people; groups of 4) cannot exclude a modest rise; the two that found about two and three times the controls' break rates (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12) had no samples from before LSD, did not describe recruitment and reported no statistical comparison, and in the larger of them every LSD patient had taken other drugs or medicines and 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so the excess cannot be attributed to LSD; and the cell studies reported no statistical test and no consistent concentration–response. Of the human studies that reported raised breakage, Irwin & Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) are now read in full; they leave the inconsistency and risk-of-bias judgments as they were, with the explanation of the positive findings now resting partly on first-hand data. The study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968) and the two laboratories' later studies enter only as the review describes them. The review is not independent of one negative study: its second author was the first author of Loughman et al. (1967), and its tables include the authors' own unpublished study. Where the review's figures differ from the primary papers, the primary papers are used: Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients and 5 volunteers, not 37 patients; one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate; the 5 volunteers' final average is 3.17% in the paper's own Table 4, not the printed 3.57% (editors' calculation); Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s cell study, which the review lists as significant, reports no test; Irwin and Egozcue print no group means, and their table gives 23.6 and 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation), not the review's 23.4% and 11.0% (11.9% in its table); Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say where their patients' LSD came from, report no test for their cells in a dish, and their Table 5 sums to 7735 treated cells, not 8725; and the review's statement that no positive study showed a relation with dose does not fit Irwin and Egozcue's own table, in which the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate in 8 people (editors' calculation). Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say whether their case 37, who matches Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s single patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, is the same man; if so, the review counts him both among people given pharmaceutical LSD and among people exposed to illicit LSD. The claim reports what was measured and where raised breakage was seen, so that a reader can see that the early reports came from people using many drugs and medicines and were not confirmed by the other teams; it does not adopt the review's closing statement that the authors believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man, which goes beyond the review's own findings that no significant work on cancer had been reported and that the human data on birth defects were case reports and one series. The cross-study tallies (14.29% against 48.9%) compare different laboratories and criteria and are not used as a rate ratio. Fly and animal findings are labelled and not used for people. Status mixed: the studies disagree, and the explanation offered for the positive findings (other drugs and medicines, street-drug contents, infections, culture methods) is plausible, and supported in one study by a small comparison group, but not established. The new anchors are not yet checked by a second reader, and studies after 1970 were not read and could change the claim. The statement gives no doses.

lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
lines.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.
